title: I Do, We Do, You Do - Or Do We?
author: Mark Enser
summary: Enser argues that gradual release -- 'I do, we do, you do' -- is a sound, well-evidenced instructional principle that is routinely hollowed out in practice. He describes lessons where the 'I do' phase becomes repeated modeling of a finished product rather than narrated expert thinking, the 'we do' phase collapses into a second teacher-led model with pupils offering only occasional words, and the 'you do' phase becomes copying with decreasing scaffolding rather than genuine independent thinking. His core diagnostic claim is that the technique isn't broken, the implementation is: teachers keep the scaffold up too long out of anxiety about a class, which makes pupils more dependent rather than more secure. He offers self-check questions for each phase -- am I showing a product or a process; who is doing the cognitive work; is the task asking pupils to think or just to recall and reproduce -- as a practical corrective. The piece closes by reframing errors that emerge in 'you do' as valuable diagnostic data rather than embarrassments, and insists gradual release requires genuine release of responsibility to be more than 'modelling with extra steps.'
points: Enser's central diagnostic is that 'I do, we do, you do' frequently degrades into 'I do, I do, I do' -- repeated teacher modeling followed by pupils copying a near-identical version, with little actual pupil thinking happening.

The 'I do' phase should function as a window into expert thinking (narrating why this word, why this evidence, what was considered and rejected), not simply a finished product for pupils to admire and replicate.

The instinct to extend scaffolding for anxious classes backfires: keeping the scaffold up longer does not make pupils more secure, it makes them more dependent, and the necessary struggle is itself a sign learning is beginning, not that teaching has failed.

Enser offers three concrete self-check questions teachers can use in real time -- in 'I do,' are you revealing process or showing product; in 'we do,' who is doing the cognitive work; in 'you do,' is the task asking pupils to think or merely recall and reproduce.
quotes: I have lost count of the number of lessons I have visited recently where what was described as “I do, we do, you do” was, in practice, something closer to “I do, I do, I do.
The point of the “I do” phase is not simply to show pupils what the finished product looks like. It is to make the thinking behind it visible.

Done poorly, as I see more often than I would like, it becomes a second model. The teacher completes most of the work, pupils offer the occasional word or phrase when prompted, and the class produces something that is still, essentially, the teacher’s.

But keeping the scaffold up too long does not make pupils more secure. It makes them more dependent. At some point, the struggle has to happen, and that struggle is not a sign that teaching has failed. It is the sign that learning is beginning.
The teacher’s job at this point is not to disappear but to circulate, observe, and make decisions about what needs addressing next. The errors that emerge are not embarrassments. They are data.
Gradual release works. But gradual release without genuine release is just modelling with extra steps, and our pupils deserve better than that.
